analogy.span: The vaccine is like giving your immune system a “wanted poster.” It doesn’t contain the criminal — just a picture of the criminal’s face. Your immune system studies the picture so it knows what to look for later.

first_move.span: The Federal Reserve doesn’t directly set every interest rate in the economy.
first_move.label: answers

last_move.span: The Federal Reserve sets interest rates mainly by choosing a target range for the federal funds rate and then using tools like interest on bank reserves, reverse repos, and lending facilities to keep actual short-term rates near that target.
last_move.label: summary

analogy.span:
Think of the Fed as setting the thermostat for the economy.

If the economy is overheating and inflation is too high, the Fed turns the heat down by raising interest rates. Borrowing gets more expensive, spending cools, and price pressures ease.

If the economy is too cold and unemployment is rising, the Fed turns the heat up by lowering interest rates. Borrowing gets cheaper, spending increases, and economic activity strengthens.

The problem is that the Fed can’t control the temperature instantly. Interest rate changes take time to work through the economy.

names_flaws.span: Taking a photo of a fridge and automatically understanding it is technically difficult.
Current AI vision is good, but not reliably perfect for this.
If the app confidently says “you have salmon” when it’s actually chicken, users may lose trust quickly.
A photo may show eggs, but not how many. It may see spinach, but not whether it’s about to spoil.
If the app says “buy eggs” when the user already has eggs, it will feel dumb.
A meal planner can be used once and abandoned unless it creates a habit.

verdict.span: Yes — it can be a good idea, but the “magic” version is harder than it sounds.
